newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore's DBS Bank profit jumps 12.6 pct in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Singapore's DBS Bank profit jumps 12.6 pct in 1996.

text.p: The Development Bank of Singapore Ltd (DBS) announced on Thursday a 12.6 percent jump in group net profits to Singapore S669.5 million (US$471.3 million) for 1996, up from S$594.6 million in 1995.

The bank said in a statement that group net interest income rose 10.2 percent to S$863.3 million, compared with S$783.2 million the year before. Group earnings per share rose to 97 cents in 1996 from 88 cents, it said.

Analysts had expected DBS, Singapore's largest bank in terms of assets, to report a 13 percent rise in group net profit to around Singapore $670 million. Estimates had varied between S$624.0 million and S$691.1 million.
DBS President Ng Kee Choe said the bank was on track for Singapore $1.0 billion in net profit by the year 2000 and predicted steady double-digit profit growth annually for the next few years.
"We expect...to achieve double-digit growth every year to the year 2000," Ng told reporters.

Ng said the bank expected growth in its core Singapore domestic market in 1997, where he predicted the economy would expand by around 7.5 percent, compared with seven percent in 1996. He also expected more growth from overseas.
"At the moment more than 30 percent of our revenue comes from overseas," he said. "We expect this proportion of income from overseas to increase over time." He gave no details.

The bank's total loans and advances grew by 17.5 percent in 1996 to a total of Singapore $32.33 billion. This rate of growth was slightly better than the average growth of 16.5 percent in total Singapore bank loans.
Ng said he thought Singapore banks' loans growth would slow slightly in 1997, but would still remain in double-digits.
Part of the reason for the slower growth would be government measures, announced in May 1996, to curb speculation in the Singapore property market.

Ng said these measures, which banned Singapore dollar loans for property purchases to foreigners and imposed new taxes on some profits from property sales, had not had an effect on the banking industry in 1996.
"We do not expect to see that until the second half of 1997," he said. Ng said he thought the weaker demand for housing loans would be "more than compensated for by growth in other areas".
Several DBS subsiidairies turned in much better results in 1996, including its brokerage arm DBS Securities, which saw profits more than double.
Ng said DBS Securities' growth had been spurred by active stock markets across the region, particularly in Hong Kong.
DBS proposed a final dividend of eight Singapore cents per share, unchanged from 1995, and a preferntial dividend of three cents, up from 2.25 cents in 1995.
